spans.text: One of my hardcovers is on sale right now with its spine printed upside down.

Not misaligned. Not slightly off. The title reads bottom to top, so on a shelf, among books whose spines all read the other way, it is the one facing the wrong direction. The spine is the only part of a hardcover a browsing reader ever sees.

It passed every check. The geometry is exact to the thousandth. Every element clears every published limit. The proof looked completely normal, and my own automated checker gave it a clean report, because that checker measures distances and an upside-down spine has perfect distances. There is no measurement that catches it. There never will be. It is not a distance.
I found it by reading the spine, months after it went on sale.
The rejections are the cheap failures
Most guides to self-publishing teach you the upload wizard: which button, which field, which order. That is worth knowing for about a week, and then you know it.
What nobody teaches is the part that actually costs money, which is that the expensive defects are not the ones that get rejected.
A rejection is inconvenient and it is also a gift. The platform looked at your file, found the problem, told you what it was, and refused to print it. You lose a day. Nothing reaches a reader.

The defects in this book are the other kind. They pass validation, they pass review, they get printed, and they arrive in someone’s hands. Some of them sit on live listings for months while every dashboard you own reports that everything is fine.
Two more, quickly
A title plate that printed
“THE SURPRISE BOO”

. The illustrated plates in that book were 5.833 inches wide against a text frame of 4.375 inches, so a third of every plate lay outside the page and was silently cropped away at print time. The contents page lost its entire page-number column, and its header was clipped to
“PA”

Nothing errored. The page count looked plausible. Every check I ran locally passed, because the file was internally consistent and simply did not fit the paper. The platform’s own previewer found it. I had not thought to look there.
Notice how small the visible damage is next to the size of the error. A third of the image is missing and what a reader sees is a dropped letter. A catastrophic layout failure presents as a typo.

A cover published broken because a spreadsheet said it was fine. Checking twenty six covers for text intruding where text must not go, I wrote a script rather than looking at twenty six covers. Then a second script, then a third. Five of them, over two days. Every one gave wrong answers, in both directions: some missed real defects, and one flagged all twenty six good files.
The damage was not the wrong answers. It was that the numbers let me sort books into buckets, and one book landed in
“moderate, not worth rebuilding on spec.”
It was published with a defective wrap and written up in my notes as ready to re-upload.
Nobody decided to ship that book broken. The bucket decided.
What they have in common
Three defects, three different mechanisms, one shape.
In each case the system reported success. In each case there was something a person could have seen in seconds, and in each case nobody looked, because a check had already said it was fine.
That is the subject of this book. Not how to use the wizard. How to find the things the wizard is happy about.

There is a version of this that overcorrects into paranoia, and I have paid for that too. Ten titles once went on hold for a hinge violation measured against a threshold I had invented, stricter than the platform’s real one. Nine of them were fine. A check you make up is not a safer check; it just fails in the other direction and teaches you to distrust the findings that are real.
So the rule this book actually argues for is narrower and more useful than
“check everything”

Trust a check that demands exact equality against a known-good reference. Distrust anything with a threshold or a bucket. And look at the thing itself, because no check can test a failure mode nobody imagined.
One number that should worry you
Here is the piece of evidence I would put in front of anyone who thinks passing review means their file is correct.

Two of my books were built with an inside margin set to exactly the platform’s stated minimum. Measured page by page against the actual ink, fifty one pages in one volume and thirty nine in the other came in under that minimum, because glyphs overhang their line boxes and the margin is measured against ink rather than against your paragraph settings.
The platform flagged one of those pages. The other fifty measured a two-thousandth of an inch under the requirement, and passed.

They passed by half of one thousandth of an inch. That file was not compliant. It was lucky, fifty separate times, and any reflow anywhere in the book would have turned some of those pages into failures.
Acceptance is not correctness. The platform accepting your file tells you the platform could not find a reason to refuse it. It is not a statement about your book.
What this is, and how to use it

This is a production manual for print books on KDP and IngramSpark, in paperback and hardcover, built out of the defect log of a working catalogue. Every measurement in it came off a real file or a real live record. Where a number was derived rather than measured, I say so. Where I got something wrong and later corrected it, the correction is in the text, because the wrong version is usually the more instructive half.

It is organised in the order the work happens. Part I covers the decisions that lock and cannot be revised. Part II is the interior, Part III the paperback cover, Part IV hardcover, and Part V IngramSpark. Part VI is the shortest and the one I would keep if I could keep only one, because it is about verification, which is the only skill here that survives a platform redesign. Part VII covers metadata and the listing.
Every chapter ends with three lines: the rule, why it bites, and how to check. Read it through once, then use those as reference.

You will not need all of it. You will need the parts that apply to the book you are making now, and you will not know which parts those are until something goes wrong, which is the argument for reading it before that happens rather than afterwards.
Three things are worth knowing before you start, because they determine how much weight to put on any given page.

Everything here was measured, not researched. This book is not a survey of what other people say about print production. It is the defect log of a working catalogue of more than seventy titles across two printers, in paperback and hardcover. Every number came off a real file, a real live record, a platform’s own template, or its own calculator. Where a value was derived rather than measured, the text says so and shows the working.

Sample sizes are stated honestly. Some findings here rest on dozens of titles and some rest on three. Where a conclusion is supported by a small sample, I say how small, and where the evidence contradicts an attractive theory, I say that too rather than quietly leaving the theory standing. Chapter 20 rests on seven measurements across two paper stocks and tells you so in its own text. Chapter 25 describes a block whose cause I never established, and says that plainly instead of guessing.

The corrections are in the text on purpose. Several chapters record a belief I held, acted on, and later disproved. Chapter 11 derived a barcode position from a constant it trusted and was wrong by 0.43 inches. Chapter 24 repeated a printer’s own published turnaround estimate that turned out to be pessimistic by an order of magnitude. Chapter 17 describes a taxonomy I built twice and revised twice.

Those are not confessions. They are the most useful parts of the book. A correct rule tells you what to do; a rule that was wrong and got fixed tells you what the wrong version looked like from the inside, which is the thing you need in order to recognise it when it is your own reasoning rather than mine.

The measurements will age. Platforms revise specifications and redesign forms. What is intended to outlast them is Part VI, which is about how to tell whether something is true rather than about any particular value being true today.
The first irreversible decision you make about a book is which ISBN it carries, and the reason it trips people up is that the question does not have one answer per book. It has one answer per format.
Paperback, ebook and hardcover are three separate products with three separate identifiers, and what you decide for one tells you nothing about the others.
The three answers
Paperback: your own ISBN, on both print rails. Buy it from your national agency, register it to the title, and use that same number on KDP and on IngramSpark.
Kindle ebook: no ISBN at all. Amazon assigns an ASIN and that is the identifier. Buying an ISBN for a Kindle edition spends money on something nothing will use.

Hardcover: the platform’s free ISBN, unless you already own one for that title. KDP hardcovers use KDP’s free ISBN, and there is no benefit to spending an owned number on a format you may only ever sell through one channel.

Two of my earliest titles are exceptions, because they had hardcover ISBNs assigned before that policy existed. Registered assignments are permanent, so those two keep theirs. Which is the next point.
Why your own ISBN on both print rails
The practical payoff is that one interior serves both platforms.

The ISBN prints on the copyright page. If KDP and IngramSpark carry different numbers for the same paperback, you need two interiors that differ by one line, forever, and every future correction has to be made twice and staged twice. Chapters 27 through 29 should be enough to convince you that maintaining two nearly identical files is a defect factory.
One owned ISBN on both rails means one file, one copyright page, one thing to fix.
A free ISBN is not a shortcut, it is a fork
Here is the consequence people do not anticipate, and it is commercial rather than technical.

If a title is already on IngramSpark under your own ISBN and you then publish it on KDP using KDP’s free ISBN, you have not saved yourself a step. You have created a second Amazon listing beside the first.

Two listings for one book split your reviews between them, split your sales rank, and compete for the buy box. Everything chapters 20 and 21 cost you in geometry is trivial next to quietly dividing your own reviews in half, particularly early on when you have very few.
So when an owned ISBN gives you trouble at setup, and the next section covers exactly when it will, do not reach for the free ISBN as an escape hatch. Fix the actual problem.
The registration is permanent, and it is the master
Once an ISBN is assigned to a title at your agency, that assignment is permanent. Never remap a number to a different book.

More usefully: your agency’s record is the source of truth, and everything else conforms to it rather than the other way round. Your local metadata files conform to it. Your interiors conform to it. Even the distributor’s dashboard conforms to it.

That is not a theoretical ranking. When I audited my own catalogue against the agency register, roughly thirty local front matter and metadata files carried wrong or placeholder ISBNs, and some of them carried another book’s real number.

That is worse than a placeholder. A placeholder is obviously wrong the moment anybody looks. A real ISBN belonging to a different book of yours passes every format check, looks entirely plausible, and prints.
Check numbers against the register before writing them anywhere, and treat a local file as a copy rather than a source. This is chapter 28’s argument arriving before you have even built anything.
The title-match rejection
Now the one that will actually stop you.
Adding your own ISBN on KDP’s content step can fail with
“The title registered to this ISBN does not match your title.”
It means what it says: the Book Title on your agency record differs from the Book Title on the KDP listing.
Four things are worth knowing about how that check behaves.
It compares the Book Title field only. Subtitles are not checked. One of my titles passed with a completely different subtitle on each side.

It is case insensitive, and on save KDP rewrites your title to the registered casing. On one title a capital letter was silently lowercased to match the register. That is mildly annoying and genuinely useful: it is a free way to read what your agency has registered without logging in to check.

The obvious fix is the wrong one. The instinct is to correct the agency record, since that is the master. I did that, and more than twenty four hours later KDP was still enforcing the old value. Agency edits propagate to retailers on their own schedule and you cannot wait it out inside a publishing session.

Change the KDP title instead. A draft’s Book Title is freely editable until roughly seventy two hours after publication, so on an unpublished draft you can simply set it to whatever the register says and the ISBN saves on the first attempt. On one title I moved the leftover words into the subtitle, which is not checked, and published in the same sitting.

One consequence to keep in mind: if you later corrected the agency record too, and that correction eventually propagates, the two will diverge again. KDP only validates at the moment the ISBN is added, so an already-published title is not at risk, but decide which value you actually want and make both sides say it.
Prefer editing the platform whenever the draft is unpublished. Fixing the register is only the better lever when the platform title is already live and locked.
When an exception is correct
Not every mismatch is a mistake, and reconciling things that were meant to differ is its own defect class.

Legacy editions. A title first published before you owned ISBNs will carry whatever number it was published under. That number stays. Do not migrate it to your own block, because migrating means unpublishing and recreating, which loses the ASIN and every review attached to it.
Single-rail titles. The both-rails rule exists to keep one interior serving two platforms. A title published only on KDP has no second rail to match, so a free ISBN there breaks nothing.

One book, two print records. The same text can legitimately appear as a KDP paperback on one number and an IngramSpark paperback on another, when those are two editions of one work rather than two books. I have a title in exactly that state, and it caused me a real error: finding a paperback carrying its own separate ISBN, I concluded there was no ebook edition and blocked a marketing campaign on that basis. There was an ebook, on a single ASIN, exactly where it should have been.
Two records is not two books. Chapter 27 makes the same point about trim sizes, where one title deliberately carries different trims on its two rails. Before you
“fix”
a divergence, establish whether somebody chose it.
One thing to check before the ISBN goes anywhere
If you intend to put a title on IngramSpark under your own ISBN, confirm that KDP’s Expanded Distribution is off before that ISBN ever reaches KDP.

Turning it on registers your number into Ingram’s database from Amazon’s side, and IngramSpark will then refuse to let you set up your own title on it. Turning it back off does not undo this. Chapter 2 covers the full mechanism, and chapter 22 covers the thirty day remedy, but the decision belongs here, at the beginning, because it is free now and expensive later.

The rule. The ISBN question is answered per format, not per book: your own number on both print rails, no ISBN for a Kindle edition, and the platform’s free number for hardcover unless you already own one.

Why it bites. A free ISBN on a title that is already on another rail creates a second competing listing that splits your reviews, and agency registrations are permanent, so a number assigned to the wrong title stays wrong.

How to check. Verify every number against your agency register rather than a local file, since a wrong ISBN that belongs to another of your books will pass every plausibility check. When KDP rejects an owned ISBN on a title mismatch, edit the KDP title rather than the register, because only one of those takes effect today. And confirm Expanded Distribution is off before an owned ISBN reaches KDP at all.

On a KDP paperback’s rights and pricing page there is a checkbox called Expanded Distribution. It offers to push your book beyond Amazon, to other retailers, wholesalers and libraries, at no cost to you.
It reads like free reach. For one specific kind of title it is a permanent, unrecoverable decision, and you have to make it before you publish rather than after.
What it actually does

Expanded Distribution does not conjure a new sales channel. Amazon feeds your title into Ingram’s catalogue, which is the wholesale system most of those other retailers and libraries actually order from.
That is a sensible service and it works. The complication is what it does to your ISBN.
Turning it on registers your ISBN into Ingram’s database with Amazon named as the publisher of record. Not you. Amazon Digital Services.
Why that is a trapdoor

If you later go to IngramSpark to set up that same title yourself, IngramSpark refuses, telling you the print ISBN is already in use. There is no duplicate record in your account. The block is arriving from the feed Amazon sent on your behalf.
The obvious remedy is to switch Expanded Distribution off and try again. It does not work, and I want to be precise about why, because I wasted a week assuming otherwise.

Unchecking stops future feeds. It does not retract the registration already pushed. There is no propagation delay to wait out, because nothing is in flight. I confirmed the republish had fully committed, with the KDP paperback reading Live and no pending changes, and the IngramSpark setup still failed with the identical message.

Then I argued the case with IngramSpark support directly: the ISBN is registered to me at the agency, Expanded Distribution is already off, there is only one record in my account, and there is no second publisher anywhere in the picture. The argument was refused. Ingram’s system shows the title as published by Amazon, and turning the setting off does not change that.

So the checkbox is one directional. Ticking it takes about a second. Undoing its consequences is a thirty day title transfer process, described in chapter 22, which IngramSpark’s own paperwork responds to by suggesting you buy a different ISBN instead.
Who this actually affects
This is the part that determines whether you need to care, and it is cleaner than it first appears.

If your paperback uses a free KDP ISBN, there is no trapdoor. A platform-assigned ISBN belongs to Amazon and was never going to appear on IngramSpark under your account regardless. Expanded Distribution on such a title is an ordinary reach decision with no hidden cost, and you can enable it or not on the merits.
If your paperback uses your own ISBN, the decision is permanent. Your number is the one asset that lets the same book exist on both rails, and Expanded Distribution spends it.

Chapter 1 recommends your own ISBN on both print rails. This chapter is the bill that arrives with that recommendation: owning the number gives you the option, and one checkbox can take the option away.
The decision, stated properly

Expanded Distribution and a direct IngramSpark listing are two routes to the same shelf. Both end with your paperback available to order through Ingram. You are choosing which of them carries your book, and for a title on your own ISBN you must choose exactly once.

Choose Expanded Distribution when: you want wider availability with no additional work, no second dashboard, no separate cover file in a different colour space, and no second set of geometry to maintain. It is genuinely less effort, and for many titles that is the right trade.

Choose a direct IngramSpark listing when: you want control over the things Expanded Distribution does not give you. Your own pricing and trade discount per market, returnability settings, hardcover and casebound options that KDP does not offer, and a listing that shows you as publisher rather than Amazon.

For most of my catalogue the direct listing wins, largely because print sales through Ingram have consistently outperformed the Amazon rail, and control over international pricing is worth real money as chapter 19 shows. But it is a genuine trade, not an obvious one, and a title you will never work on again is a perfectly good candidate for the checkbox.
What you cannot do is defer the decision. Publishing with Expanded Distribution on and deciding later is choosing.
Check before the ISBN goes anywhere near KDP
The practical rule is stricter than
“decide before publishing,”
because the setting can be enabled during setup without much ceremony.

Confirm Expanded Distribution is off before your owned ISBN reaches KDP at all, on any title you might ever want on IngramSpark. It costs one look at the rights and pricing page. Once the feed has fired you are into the thirty day queue with a publication date you have already chosen and probably announced.
And push any publication date on a title in that state by a month rather than by days. The remedy runs on Ingram’s schedule, not yours.
Audit what you already published
If you have a back catalogue, this is worth an afternoon.

Any live title with Expanded Distribution enabled will hit this block the moment you attempt its IngramSpark listing, and you will find out at the worst possible time, with files built and a date set. The setting sits on each paperback’s rights and pricing page, so the audit is mechanical: open each title, look, write it down.

Titles you have no intention of putting on IngramSpark can stay as they are. For anything you might expand later, switching the setting off now at least stops further feeds, even though it will not clear a registration that has already gone.
In my own catalogue exactly one title had been left with it enabled, against a house default of off. One title was enough to cost a month.

The rule. Expanded Distribution registers your ISBN into Ingram’s catalogue with Amazon as publisher of record. On a title using your own ISBN, that forecloses setting the book up on IngramSpark yourself, and unchecking the box does not undo it.

Why it bites. It presents as a free reach setting rather than as an exclusive choice between two routes to the same wholesaler, and its consequence only appears months later when you try the other route.

How to check. Decide the route before the ISBN reaches KDP, not before publication. Confirm the setting is off on any owned-ISBN title you might list on IngramSpark. Audit existing titles for it now rather than discovering it mid-launch, and treat a title already in that state as a month of delay, not a week.
